parts:
Hi all, 

I'm a Masters student and I am using the Distance R package for part of my dissertation project. I am trying to estimate gibbon density from point transect survey data. The survey consisted of six arrays of three listening posts distributed throughout one forest strata (pristine). Each array was surveyed for four days and surveyors estimated the distance to calling groups from their posts. I want to calculate the estimated group density of the gibbons using distance. I have a couple of questions about using the R package that I thought people here may be able to help with:

1. Most papers I have read which used distance sampling for analysing gibbon point transect data have measured from a single average point for each array (set of three listening posts) and an average location for each detected gibbon group. However, I have recently read a paper (DOI: 10.1002/ajp.23169) in which the researchers measured the distance from each individual listening post in an array to each detected group. Which method would people recommend for this kind of analysis? 

2. As I want to estimate the group density, I have grouped the survey data in GIS using triangulation and the call times. For example, group 1 consists of three detections (three distance estimates) made by each of the three listening posts in array 1. How can I include this in my input data for the R package? Can I just put a column for "cluster" in my distance input csv to specify that there is more than one distance recorded for most groups?

3. I have calculated the effective sampling area of my arrays in GIS prior to the distance analysis. Each array has a different effective sampling area. Can I still run distance analysis for all the arrays at the same time? Or would I have to the analysis separately for each array?

4. Do I need to specify which listening post in each array detected each group? (e.g. listening post 1 detected groups 1, 3 and 6).

5. For the survey data, I need to adjust the density estimate by the estimate of calling probability in one day. I'm a bit confused as to how I should use the dht2 function for this. I am using an Excel package to estimate the calling probability in one day of the gibbons from the survey data. The estimate gives my calling probability and it's variance. Can I just enter the calling probability as a cue rate column into my distance input file (e.g. for my data the calling probability in one day is estimated to be 0.7, so can I just put 0.7 cue rate for all the detections?)

Many thanks,
Toby

parts:
Toby

I don't claim to be an expert in analysis of gibbon acoustic detection data, but here are my thoughts on your questions.

1. My understanding is that an array will give rise to a single detection distance, measured from the centre of the array.  The reason for the multiple listening posts is to perform the triangulation to determine the location of the vocalisation.  With that location determined, the distance from the vocalisation to the centre of the array is the radial distance that will be analysed.

2. Each detection by an array is a single detection, not three records for a group detection.

3. I presume you wish to make inference to the forest stratum in which the arrays were located.  Therefore information from all arrays are analysed together.  Effective sampling area is computed across all arrays.  The exception would be if there were array-specific covariates involved in the analysis.

4. No

5. The estimated calling rate and its precision are called "multipliers".  Have a look at the vignette regarding cue count surveys (your gibbon survey) at our Examples website (http://examples.distancesampling.org/Distance-cues/cuecounts-distill.html).  In the section about `dht2` you will see how to create a named list "mult" that contains the call rate and its standard error.  The list "mult" is passed as the argument "multipliers" to the `dht2` function.  This converts density of calls to density of groups.

Hope that answers some of your questions.

Hi Eric,

For my data, each array was surveyed for four days (each day between the hours of an average of 4 am - 8 am) and the cue rate I'm using is calling probability on one day (the probability that gibbons will call on one day). In the guidance, it states that the unit of search time and the unit of the cue rate have to be the same. The cue rate is based one day, so should I do 24 hours for the cue rate and 4 hours for search time? Or should I say that the cue rate was one day and the search time was 4 days?   • If I want to estimate the effective detection radius in the R package using a maximum listening distance of 1000 m, how would I do that? I calculated an Effective Listening Area of each array for the Triangulation analysis, which I have input into the area column in my input csv for the R package, but I've seen some papers that calculate Effective Detection Radius in Distance and I was unsure whether this would be more accurate.

In addition to Distance Sampling, I’m also analysing the survey data using acoustic spatial capture-recapture (ASCR). That does not require for bearing estimates to triangulate as it factors in bearing error. Can Distance do a similar thing?

  • ·Some of the arrays are within a few hundred meters away from a different stratum that I do not want to estimate the density for (in my case I only want to estimate the density in the pristine forest area but there are two other strata in the study site: once-burnt and twice-burnt). Would a better option be to input a raster which is classified as pristine forest = 1, once-burnt/twice burnt = 0, so that I can tell the software the extent of the pristine forest and which points fall outside it?

Many thanks,
Toby

parts:
Toby

Further thoughts, my bullets correspond to your bullets--

  • Hopefully you can convert the call probability of 0.7 in a day into a rate.  Would it make sense that there were 0.7 calls in 4 hours of listening?  That could be converted to an hourly call rate of 0.175 calls per hour, eh?  You would need to adjust your measure of precision as well.
  • Yes, the value required does need to be a standard error, not a variance.
  • Effective detection radius is maximum listening distance divided by detection probability (provided in `ds()` output).
  • `ds()` cannot incorporate uncertainty in bearings in the analysis
  • I think you are describing the potential of making detections outside your "study area", in this case your pristine habitat type.  You could impose more stringent truncation of your radial distances (eliminating the most distant detections); this would be another way to solve this problem.

Hi Toby,

If I understand you correctly, I think you have a problem if you set g(0) to equal the probability of an individual gibbon (or gibbon group) calling per day. This is because whether a gibbon calls during any time in the day is far less relevant then whether it calls whenever it is at 0 distance. Imagine that an individual gibbon (or group) calls every day (so probability of calling per day is 1), but only calls for 10% of the time while at 0 distance. This would make probability of detection at 0 distance 10%.

What I think you need is the probability that a gibbon (or group) calls during each period/snapshot that you work out a density for. If your snapshots are more or less instantaneous (which would conform to classic distance sampling assumptions) then this probability is (more or less) equal to the proportion of time that gibbons spend calling (assuming calls are randomly distributed over the course of the day). If you are working on a period basis, you would have to calculate/estimate the probability of calling within that period.

Hope that makes sense!

Mark

If I understand you correctly, I think you have a problem if you set g(0) to equal the probability of an individual gibbon (or gibbon group) calling per day. What I think you need is the probability that a gibbon (or group) calls during each period/snapshot that you work out a density for. If you are working on a period basis, you would have to calculate/estimate the probability of calling within that period.

Hope that makes sense!

If I understand you correctly, I think you have a problem if you set g(0) to equal the probability of an individual gibbon (or gibbon group) calling per day. This is because whether a gibbon calls during any time in the day is far less relevant then whether it calls whenever it is at 0 distance. Imagine that an individual gibbon (or group) calls every day (so probability of calling per day is 1), but only calls for 10% of the time while at 0 distance. This would make probability of detection at 0 distance 10%.

 

What I think you need is the probability that a gibbon (or group) calls during each period/snapshot that you work out a density for. If your snapshots are more or less instantaneous (which would conform to classic distance sampling assumptions) then this probability is (more or less) equal to the proportion of time that gibbons spend calling (assuming calls are randomly distributed over the course of the day). If you are working on a period basis, you would have to calculate/estimate the probability of calling within that period.

 

Hope that makes sense!

Hi Toby,

 

If I understand you correctly, I think you have a problem if you set g(0) to equal the probability of an individual gibbon (or gibbon group) calling per day. This is because whether a gibbon calls during any time in the day is far less relevant then whether it calls whenever it is at 0 distance. Imagine that an individual gibbon (or group) calls every day (so probability of calling per day is 1), but only calls for 10% of the time while at 0 distance. This would make probability of detection at 0 distance 10%.

 

What I think you need is the probability that a gibbon (or group) calls during each period/snapshot that you work out a density for. If your snapshots are more or less instantaneous (which would conform to classic distance sampling assumptions) then this probability is (more or less) equal to the proportion of time that gibbons spend calling (assuming calls are randomly distributed over the course of the day). If you are working on a period basis, you would have to calculate/estimate the probability of calling within that period.

 

Hope that makes sense!

 

Mark

On Friday, 11 September 2020 at 11:35:19 UTC+1 Mark Wilson wrote:

Hi Toby,

 

If I understand you correctly, I think you have a problem if you set g(0) to equal the probability of an individual gibbon (or gibbon group) calling per day. This is because whether a gibbon calls during any time in the day is far less relevant then whether it calls whenever it is at 0 distance. Imagine that an individual gibbon (or group) calls every day (so probability of calling per day is 1), but only calls for 10% of the time while at 0 distance. This would make probability of detection at 0 distance 10%.

 

What I think you need is the probability that a gibbon (or group) calls during each period/snapshot that you work out a density for. If your snapshots are more or less instantaneous (which would conform to classic distance sampling assumptions) then this probability is (more or less) equal to the proportion of time that gibbons spend calling (assuming calls are randomly distributed over the course of the day). If you are working on a period basis, you would have to calculate/estimate the probability of calling within that period.

 

Hope that makes sense!

 

Mark

Further thoughts, my bullets correspond to your bullets--

  • Hopefully you can convert the call probability of 0.7 in a day into a rate.  Would it make sense that there were 0.7 calls in 4 hours of listening?  That could be converted to an hourly call rate of 0.175 calls per hour, eh?  You would need to adjust your measure of precision as well.

On Wednesday, 2 September 2020 at 13:40:41 UTC+1 Eric Rexstad wrote:

Toby

I don't claim to be an expert in analysis of gibbon acoustic detection data, but here are my thoughts on your questions.

1. My understanding is that an array will give rise to a single detection distance, measured from the centre of the array.  The reason for the multiple listening posts is to perform the triangulation to determine the location of the vocalisation.  With that location determined, the distance from the vocalisation to the centre of the array is the radial distance that will be analysed.

2. Each detection by an array is a single detection, not three records for a group detection.

3. I presume you wish to make inference to the forest stratum in which the arrays were located.  Therefore information from all arrays are analysed together.  Effective sampling area is computed across all arrays.  The exception would be if there were array-specific covariates involved in the analysis.

4. No

5. The estimated calling rate and its precision are called "multipliers".  Have a look at the vignette regarding cue count surveys (your gibbon survey) at our Examples website (http://examples.distancesampling.org/Distance-cues/cuecounts-distill.html).  In the section about `dht2` you will see how to create a named list "mult" that contains the call rate and its standard error.  The list "mult" is passed as the argument "multipliers" to the `dht2` function.  This converts density of calls to density of groups.

Hope that answers some of your questions.
